: **The running machine's card**: The fifteen parameters of the warehouse mobile manipulator that later calculations use most. A derived value built on illustrative inputs is illustrative evidence. Values print from the MLSysIM registry when the book is built. {#tbl-01-machine-card tbl-colwidths="[24,12,12,52]"}

With these parameters fixed, every subsequent design problem on this platform begins from the same physical foundation: identify which margin the commanded action approaches, and determine whether the system can execute an assured protective response before that margin is exhausted. Whether a given physical deployment also requires the learned policies and delegated-authority architecture developed throughout this book is a separate question, addressed by the scope test in the next section.

## The Physical AI Scope Test {#sec-boundary-scope-test}

A robotic arm in a fulfillment center can track a fixed proportional-integral-derivative profile, execute an offline trajectory pre-screened and loaded by a human technician, or stream joint torques directly from a learned policy running on real-time sensor frames. While all three regimes actuate identical electric motors and gear trains, they impose fundamentally different architectural obligations on the computing system. The scope test establishes the operational boundaries that define physical AI throughout this book.

The scope of physical AI is defined by the simultaneous intersection of three structural criteria:

1. **Learned Statistical Model:** The system relies on a policy, perception encoder, or world model whose runtime behavior emerges from training data rather than an inspectable closed-form specification, as seen in deep neural networks or diffusion policies [@chi2024diffusionpolicy]. Correctness cannot be formally proven across all state configurations from source code alone; engineers must establish operational validity empirically across a defined operating domain. By contrast, a linear plant model fitted through classical system identification,[^fn-sysid-scope-test] where parameter uncertainty yields provable stability margins, falls outside this category. A high-capacity neural policy falls squarely within it.
2. **Consequential Physical Feedback:** Actuator commands alter the material state of the surrounding physical world, and those state changes directly govern what onboard sensors measure in subsequent time steps under classical mechanics, thermodynamics, or electromagnetism. The environment cannot be paused or rolled back: energy dissipated into the physical world cannot be recalled.
3. **Delegated Physical Authority (System-Level Actuation):** A learned component's output—whether a raw percept, a semantic state estimate, or a proposed motion trajectory—can propagate to live physical actuators without requiring synchronous human approval for each control cycle. The learned network need not write directly to motor driver registers; the system possesses delegated authority whenever learned signals actively shape downstream actuation commands. Adding downstream safety checks or deterministic rate limiters does not vacate this authority, provided accepted proposals still drive hardware motion. Furthermore, an automated monitor that validates action candidates using the same learned perception pipeline provides no true independence: a single perceptual misclassification can corrupt both the candidate trajectory and the safety check simultaneously.

Together, these three criteria delineate the domain of physical AI. The three-set Venn diagram in @fig-01-scope-venn formalizes this boundary, locating physical AI at the central intersection where learned models, continuous physical feedback, and automated physical authority converge. The pairwise overlaps isolate advisory systems (learned models with feedback but without execution authority), digital autonomy (learned models with software authority but lacking physical plant dynamics), and classical control (closed-loop physical actuation governed by analytical laws rather than statistical models).

[^fn-sysid-scope-test]: **System Identification**: The control-engineering practice of fitting low-order dynamic models to measured input-output time series. Because classical system identification produces bounded parameter uncertainties, control theorists can construct provable stability guarantees before deploying the controller. In contrast, modern high-dimensional neural representations lack tractable closed-form uncertainty bounds, requiring empirical verification across explicitly specified operational domains. \index{System identification!scope test}

::: {#fig-01-scope-venn fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The physical AI scope test**: Physical AI combines a learned component, consequential physical feedback, and system-level authority to let learned outputs reach actuation without human approval. An independent veto belongs inside this intersection because accepted proposals can still move the plant. The pairwise overlaps locate advisory systems, digital autonomy, and classical control." fig-alt="Three-set Venn diagram defining physical AI at the intersection of learned models, physical feedback, and physical authority. The pairwise overlaps show advisory systems, digital autonomy, and classical control."}
![](images/svg/fig01_scope_venn.svg){width="90%"}
:::

Examining systems that satisfy only two of these criteria highlights why each dimension demands distinct engineering practices. A classical proportional-integral-derivative (PID) speed governor operates in a tight closed loop under relentless physical feedback, yet relies entirely on analytical control laws rather than learned statistical models. At another extreme, an automated algorithmic trading engine processes millions of learned market forecasts and executes real-time financial transactions; while highly consequential, its closed loop unfolds entirely across digital networks rather than through physical work governed by Newtonian dynamics. Excluding these architectures from physical AI circumscribes our design problem to systems where statistical uncertainty directly collides with physical irreversibility.

A learned model alone does not make a machine a physical AI system. Consider an offline trajectory generator that optimizes smooth paths using a learned diffusion model. If a manufacturing engineer must inspect, validate, and load those toolpaths onto a Computer Numerical Control (CNC) mill prior to cutting metal, the statistical model operates strictly as an advisory tool. The human retains ultimate physical authority. Similarly, a vision model that highlights defects on an assembly line display assists human inspection without closing the physical loop.

Conversely, delegated authority does not require end-to-end neural control. Most production autonomous systems adopt modular architectures where deep neural networks handle perception while deterministic trajectory planners compute actual actuator setpoints. These systems satisfy the physical authority test through perception: if an unvetted object detection or bounding-box estimate triggers an automated swerve or emergency braking maneuver, the learned representation directly dictates plant dynamics. The autonomous test vehicle in the Tempe collision discussed in @sec-boundary-when-fails exemplifies this failure mode, where misclassifications in modular perception cascaded into catastrophic actuation decisions.

Shared autonomy falls squarely within physical AI whenever a learned sub-system modifies live motion before a human operator can intervene. In a robotic surgical console equipped with learned haptic virtual fixtures, for example, the assistive policy exerts real forces on the master tool manipulators to guide the surgeon around delicate anatomical structures. Even if the surgeon holds administrative responsibility for the procedure, high-bandwidth force cues alter physical tissue contact well within normal human neurological reaction latency (typically 150 ms to 250 ms). Because the machine enforces learned spatial guidance dynamically without requiring the surgeon to review and acknowledge each micro-correction, it exercises delegated physical authority in the physical domain.

When classifying an ambiguous machine, engineers must evaluate each of the three criteria independently. Implementing an independent deterministic veto—such as an analog brake relay triggered by a certified safety lidar—does not strip a machine of delegated authority, because learned proposals still govern all nominal motion up to the intervention threshold. In contrast, requiring a human operator to screen and authorize every trajectory command before transmission reliably removes that authority. Once a design satisfies all three criteria, it qualifies as physical AI, and its computing architecture must respect the hard timing and causal boundaries established in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary.

::: {#chk-boundary-scope-test .callout-checkpoint title="Binding budgets and the scope test"}

- [ ] **Delay vs. braking**: Can you explain why response delay and active braking consume separate portions of stopping clearance, and which one dominates above the crossover speed?
- [ ] **Stopping budget estimate**: Using the machine card, can you estimate how far the elementary stop at the `{python} StoppingBudget.v_str` drive limit grows if the `{python} StoppingBudget.t_lease_str` chunk lease doubles, and whether it still fits inside the `{python} StoppingBudget.d_clear_str` clear distance?
- [ ] **Binding margins**: Can you identify the relevant physical margin when the warehouse machine travels, presses a latch, and holds a load?
- [ ] **Scope criteria**: Can you apply all three scope criteria to a new machine, including one whose learned output passes through an independent veto?

:::

Satisfying the scope test binds statistical uncertainty directly to hardware consequences. To design systems that operate safely under these demands, computer systems engineers must map how timing, state estimation, and control authority distribute along the execution path from raw sensor frames to physical actuator motion.

## The Machine in Five Levels {#sec-boundary-machine-model}

An embodied machine requires an architecture that prevents unverified, learned models from writing directly to the actuators they could damage, while still granting those models the authority to guide physical behavior.

The Body establishes what motion, force, and mechanical power the hardware can physically sustain. The Brain generates learned proposals intended to operate within those capabilities. Mediating between them, the Nervous System coordinates communication and control, preserving both the temporal margin and the hardware authority required to intercept and refuse an inadmissible command. We organize these responsibilities into a five-level model spanning learned computation down to the physical environment:

1. **The Brain (Level 1):** The learned models that interpret sensory observations and propose candidate goals, trajectories, or torques. Generating a proposed trajectory or sequence of setpoints confers no intrinsic authority to execute it.
2. **The Nervous System (Level 2):** The deterministic communication buses, real-time schedulers, and control loops that bridge proposals to physical execution. Its permission path evaluates, filters, or rejects proposals against fresh sensory evidence and invariant physical limits, and it executes a guaranteed safe fallback whenever the proposer falters.
3. **The Body (Level 3):** The physical plant—including motor drives, transmissions, electromagnetic windings, structural linkages, and energy storage—that delivers mechanical action.
4. **The Boundary (Level 4):** The hard physical and electrical interface where digital registers translate into actuator voltages or currents, and where physical phenomena register across sensor transducers as raw measurements.
5. **The World (Level 5):** The external physical environment—surfaces, payloads, obstacles, ambient lighting, and human collaborators—which evolves continuously under the laws of physics regardless of whether the machine measures it.

A concrete physical AI implementation often maps this hierarchy across distinct computational tiers: learned proposers run on high-throughput accelerator hosts (such as an application processor paired with a GPU or neural processing unit), the permission path executes on an independent real-time microcontroller or dedicated real-time operating system core, and the field-oriented current loops run directly on dedicated motor drives. This architectural isolation is rooted in strict timing guarantees and fault-containment boundaries rather than specific silicon families or nominal operating system labels.

Governance does not constitute a sixth level in this real-time control hierarchy. Instead, it serves as the operational and lifecycle envelope enclosing all five. Governance determines which entity holds valid command authority, what verification evidence licenses the machine to operate, and when those operational leases expire. Crucially, governance transitions unfold across the human and operational timescales of safety interventions, policy rollouts, and maintenance releases, rather than the millisecond rhythms of real-time control loops.

::: {#dfn-boundary-proposal-boundary .callout-definition title="Proposal boundary"}

***Proposal boundary***\index{Proposal boundary!definition}\index{Permission path!definition} is the line between a learned model, which may only propose an action, and the **permission path**, an independent mechanism with bounded latency that the model cannot delay or corrupt and that alone may permit the action to reach an actuator. The permission path validates every proposal against fresh sensory evidence, the stopping envelope (the state space from which the machine can safely decelerate to a halt prior to obstacle collision), and a certified fallback trajectory reachable from the current state. If any condition is violated, the permission path rejects the proposal immediately.

1.  **Significance**: Prevents learned model outputs from directly manipulating actuators. This architectural protection remains dependable only as long as the permission path's independent sensing, dynamic models, and fallback maneuvers remain physically valid.
2.  **Distinction**: Even a deep reinforcement learning policy trained to emit joint torques possesses zero raw actuator-write authority; its output remains a mere proposal until explicitly admitted by the permission path.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the permission path as a cosmetic post-processing filter or output clamp, rather than an autonomous supervisory mechanism capable of seizing control when the learned proposer hangs, violates deadlines, emits pathological values, or falls silent.

The proposal boundary determines who holds the authority to approve an action, whereas the causal boundary marks the physical interface where an admitted command alters the state of the plant. The Nervous System bridges this divide, verifying proposals against hard constraints before energizing the drives.

:::

Readers steeped in classical control theory will recognize this design as a supervisory architecture. Specifically, the proposal boundary implements runtime assurance. In classic Simplex architectures, a complex, high-performance controller (here, the learned policy) is paired with a certified baseline controller, coordinated by decision logic that determines which subsystem drives the plant [@seto1998simplex; @sha2001using]. @Tbl-01-law-lineage maps our terminology directly to classic control literature.

Crucially, hardware fault isolation alone does not guarantee safety: architectural independence also constrains the permission path's sensor inputs. If an enforcement monitor validates a proposed trajectory using the very same learned perception pipeline that synthesized it, a single perception error will corrupt both components simultaneously. The sensing pipelines that grant execution authority must therefore maintain distinct failure modes from the learned models they supervise.

@Fig-01-locator partitions the machine into five stacked architectural tiers, mapping each level to its characteristic control frequency and governing chapters: from the continuous physical World (bottom) up through the event-timed Boundary, the 10–25 kHz current loops of the mechanical Body, and the 1 kHz permission loops of the Nervous System, to the hierarchical Brain (operating from 40 Hz setpoints to 2 Hz intent models at the top). The prominent gap between Brain and Nervous System marks the foundational proposal boundary: components above this line may only formulate proposals, while only deterministic subsystems below it possess the authority to command physical actuators. The operating frequencies charted across the levels reflect the reference architecture analyzed throughout this book, rather than immutable physical constants for every robotic platform. Subsequent chapters derive these timing budgets directly from task dynamics and mechanical plant characteristics. What remains fundamental across all physical AI systems is the proposal boundary that severs learned computation from unchecked execution authority.

```{python}
#| label: boundary-locator-rates
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LOCATOR RATES (LEGO GUARD FOR A HAND-DRAWN FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-01-locator (fig01_machine_levels.svg) in
# │          @sec-boundary-machine-model.
# │ Goal:    Keep the rates drawn on the Brain and Nervous System bands equal to
# │          the running machine's registry values.
# │ Show:    intent model 2 Hz; chunk renewal 20 Hz; setpoints 40 Hz; 1 kHz tick.
# │ How:     Read the registry; check() fails the build if a registry change
# │          leaves the SVG labels stale. Nothing prints.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check

class LocatorRates:
    """Registry rates that fig01_machine_levels.svg draws as text."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
    f_intent = RM.intent_rate.to(hertz).magnitude  # category: chosen
    f_chunk = RM.chunk_rate.to(hertz).magnitude  # category: chosen
    f_step = (1 / RM.chunk_step).to(hertz).magnitude  # category: derived from the chosen step
    f_tick = RM.permission_rate.to(hertz).magnitude  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    drawn = {"intent": 2.0, "chunk": 20.0, "step": 40.0, "tick": 1000.0}  # labels in the SVG
    check(abs(f_intent - drawn["intent"]) < 1e-9, f"Locator draws intent at 2 Hz; registry says {f_intent}.")
    check(abs(f_chunk - drawn["chunk"]) < 1e-9, f"Locator draws chunk renewal at 20 Hz; registry says {f_chunk}.")
    check(abs(f_step - drawn["step"]) < 1e-9, f"Locator draws setpoints at 40 Hz; registry says {f_step}.")
    check(abs(f_tick - drawn["tick"]) < 1e-9, f"Locator draws a 1 kHz permission loop; registry says {f_tick}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    # Guard-only class: it pins the values drawn in the figure; no prose outputs.
```

::: {#fig-01-locator fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The five-level machine**: Each band carries its pinned rate and the chapters that work on it. The wider gap between Brain and Nervous System marks the proposal boundary, above which a component may only propose. A chapter-opening stack with no level highlighted marks a governance chapter. The permission-loop rate shown is one implementation." fig-alt="Five stacked horizontal bands labeled from top to bottom Brain (learned proposers, intent model 2 hertz, chunk renewal 20 hertz, setpoints 40 hertz), Nervous System (permission path, lease, fallback, a 1 kilohertz loop in one implementation), Body (drives, transmission, windings, rails, current loop 10 to 25 kilohertz), Boundary (register write and sensor capture, event-timed), and World (contact, friction, payload, people, continuous). A wider gap between Brain and Nervous System is labeled proposal boundary, above may only propose, below may command. A dashed outline enclosing all five bands is labeled governance, lifecycle envelope, Part IV, no control rate. Chapter numbers sit at the right edge of each band: Brain 3, 6, 8 to 11; Nervous System 4, 12, 13; Body 2; Boundary 1, 8; World 5, 7."}
![](images/svg/fig01_machine_levels.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Deploying capable physical AI requires balancing expressive policy proposals with deterministic execution guarantees. This separation of concerns does not demand rejecting every imperfect proposal out of hand; real-time intervention mechanisms can project a trajectory onto safe constraints or smoothly blend corrections, preserving task progress while strictly respecting physical invariants. Rigorous systems evaluation must therefore disentangle what the learned proposer achieves in isolation, how effectively the integrated machine executes under routine supervisory filtering, and whether the fallback mechanisms themselves introduce secondary hazards.

Distributing responsibilities across these five levels establishes the structural foundation for the remainder of this book. More importantly, it provides a principled framework for diagnosing real-world failures without reflexively reducing every physical malfunction to a deficiency in neural network weights.

## When the Responsibilities Fail Together {#sec-boundary-when-fails}

A warehouse model that recognizes an obstacle too late cannot recover the clearance already consumed. In a road vehicle, the same timing problem can combine with tracking errors, delayed intervention, and missing redundancy. The 2018 Tempe collision provides a documented example of these interacting failures; it does not establish that one prescribed hardware architecture would have prevented them. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) attributed the crash primarily to the vehicle operator's distraction. The design choices traced below explain why the automated system had made that single, unmonitored person the last line of defense.

```{python}
#| label: boundary-incident-record
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE TEMPE AND CRUISE RECORDS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-01-law-lineage and @sec-boundary-when-fails (Tempe timeline,
# │          action suppression, braking cap, Cruise pullover, checkpoint).
# │ Goal:    Print the investigators' own values once, and derive the travel
# │          during action suppression from the two recorded speeds.
# │ Show:    5.6 s first detection; 43.2 mph at 1.2 s before impact; 1 s
# │          suppression ending at 0.2 s and 40.5 mph; takeover at 0.02 s;
# │          18.7 m during suppression; 7 m/s^2 (0.71 g) chosen cap against
# │          0.92 g (9.0 m/s^2) capability; Cruise about 20 ft (6.1 m) at up
# │          to 7.7 mph.
# │ How:     Literature values from NTSB/HAR-19/03 and the Quinn Emanuel report,
# │          loaded here until the literature registry holds them. Suppression
# │          travel uses the mean of the two recorded speeds (trapezoid rule);
# │          no counterfactual stop is computed.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_math, check

class IncidentRecord:
    """Investigator-reported values for the Tempe (2018) and Cruise (2023) cases."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    # category: literature. NTSB/HAR-19/03 (2019), p. v and table pp. 15-16
    t_detect = 5.6 * second  # first detection, before impact
    t_recognize = 1.2 * second  # emergency recognized and suppression begins, before impact
    v_recognize = 43.2 * ureg.mph  # recorded speed at that instant
    t_suppress = 1.0 * second  # action-suppression period (p. 13)
    t_supp_end = 0.2 * second  # suppression ends, before impact
    v_supp_end = 40.5 * ureg.mph  # recorded speed at that instant
    t_takeover = 0.02 * second  # operator takes the wheel, before impact
    # category: literature. NTSB/HAR-19/03, p. 13 and footnote 33
    a_cap = 7.0 * meter / second**2  # ADS emergency threshold and braking cap (chosen by the developer)
    g_capable = 0.92  # police-determined average deceleration capability in the crash area, in g
    # category: literature. Quinn Emanuel report to the Cruise boards (2024), p. 10
    d_drag = 20 * ureg.foot  # approximate distance moved during the pullover
    v_drag = 7.7 * ureg.mph  # maximum speed during the pullover

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    g0 = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)
    d_suppress = (0.5 * (v_recognize + v_supp_end) * t_suppress).to(meter)
    a_cap_g = (a_cap / g0).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    a_capable = (g_capable * g0).to(meter / second**2)
    d_drag_m = d_drag.to(meter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs((t_recognize - t_supp_end - t_suppress).to(second).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Suppression must span the two table rows.")
    check(abs(a_cap_g - 0.71) < 5e-3, f"NTSB states the cap as 0.71 g, got {a_cap_g}.")
    check(a_capable > a_cap, "The chosen cap must sit below the vehicle's capability.")
    check(abs(d_suppress.magnitude - 18.7) < 0.05, f"Suppression travel is about 18.7 m, got {d_suppress}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_detect_str = fmt_latency(t_detect, unit=second, precision=1)
    t_suppress_str = fmt_latency(t_suppress, unit=second, precision=0)
    t_recognize_math = fmt_math(rf"T-{fmt(t_recognize, unit=second, precision=1)}\text{{ s}}")
    t_supp_end_math = fmt_math(rf"T-{fmt(t_supp_end, unit=second, precision=1)}\text{{ s}}")
    t_takeover_math = fmt_math(rf"T-{fmt(t_takeover, unit=second, precision=2)}\text{{ s}}")
    v_recognize_str = fmt_velocity(v_recognize, unit=ureg.mph, precision=1)
    v_supp_end_str = fmt_velocity(v_supp_end, unit=ureg.mph, precision=1)
    d_suppress_str = fmt_length(d_suppress, unit=meter, precision=1)
    a_cap_str = fmt_acceleration(a_cap, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    a_cap_g_str = fmt(a_cap_g, precision=2)
    g_capable_str = fmt(g_capable, precision=2)
    a_capable_str = fmt_acceleration(a_capable, unit=meter / second**2, precision=1)
    d_drag_str = fmt_length(d_drag, unit=ureg.foot, precision=0)
    d_drag_m_str = fmt_length(d_drag_m, unit=meter, precision=1)
    v_drag_str = fmt_velocity(v_drag, unit=ureg.mph, precision=1)
```

On a March night in 2018, a modified Volvo XC90 operating Uber Advanced Technologies Group (ATG)'s developmental automated driving system (ADS) struck and fatally injured a pedestrian pushing a bicycle across a road in Tempe, Arizona [@ntsb2019uber].[^fn-inc-tempe-investigation] The NTSB architectural profile in @fig-01-tempe-vehicle maps the developmental sensor and computing payload integrated onto the Volvo XC90 chassis: a roof-mounted lidar pod, forward and side radars, surround cameras, and rooftop GPS antennas, routed back to automated driving system (ADS) compute and data-storage racks installed in the cargo bay. The ADS first detected the pedestrian `{python} IncidentRecord.t_detect_str` before impact, but detection alone did not provide a correct path prediction [@ntsb2019uber].

[^fn-inc-tempe-investigation]: **Reading the Tempe Record**\index{2018 Tempe Autonomous Collision!NTSB report}: Times in this section count backward from impact at $\Time$, as the event table of NTSB/HAR-19/03 does, and speeds are those the ADS itself recorded [@ntsb2019uber]. The report also cautions that communication delay leaves unclear exactly when the planned slowdown began. Reading each time as an interval before impact, rather than as a clock time, is what lets it be converted into distance traveled at the recorded speed, the conversion this section applies.

::: {#fig-01-tempe-vehicle fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Tempe test vehicle sensor locations**: The NTSB diagram identifies the developmental ADS vehicle's lidar, camera, radar, computing, and telecommunications locations. (Source: NTSB, public domain)." fig-alt="NTSB side-view diagram of the Volvo test vehicle with colored outlines marking lidar, cameras, radar, ADS computing and data storage, and GPS equipment."}
![](images/jpg/fig01_real_ntsb_tempe_vehicle.jpg){width="95%"}
:::

### Tracking history loss under classification churn {#sec-boundary-tracking-churn}

Despite continuing to track the detected object, the ADS did not brake in response to it. The NTSB record shows classification changes among vehicle, bicycle, and other before `{python} IncidentRecord.t_recognize_math` [@ntsb2019uber].

When the classification changed, the ADS path predictor did not use the object's earlier locations; for an "other" object it could assume a static path.[^fn-ctrl-kalman-tracking] The loss of earlier locations matters because successive positions provide evidence of motion across the roadway. A changing semantic label must not silently discard that evidence. The resulting path predictions did not place the pedestrian in the sport utility vehicle (SUV)'s lane until `{python} IncidentRecord.t_recognize_math` [@ntsb2019uber].

[^fn-ctrl-kalman-tracking]: **Tracking-History Loss**\index{Tracking history!classification changes}: The NTSB record states only that a changed classification caused the predictor to omit the object's earlier locations; it does not describe a Kalman-filter reset or a zero-velocity initialization, so neither should be read into it [@ntsb2019uber]. The consequence follows from the omission alone. Each relabeling shortened the evidence window from which motion is estimated, so an object crossing the lane began again, after each change, as one with no recorded history of crossing.

### Action suppression and the kinematic stopping deficit {#sec-boundary-action-suppression}

The ADS included an action-suppression interval intended to reduce responses to false alarms while the system checked the situation and allowed operator intervention [@ntsb2019uber]. That software choice also consumed time available for a physical response.

At `{python} IncidentRecord.t_recognize_math`, with the vehicle traveling at `{python} IncidentRecord.v_recognize_str`, the ADS recognized an emergency and entered its one-second action-suppression period. The design withheld braking while it checked the hazard or waited for operator intervention. At `{python} IncidentRecord.t_supp_end_math`, suppression ended with the vehicle at `{python} IncidentRecord.v_supp_end_str`. The ADS then initiated a plan for gradual slowdown and sounded an alert; it did not request emergency braking. The NTSB notes that communication delay leaves unclear whether that slowdown began before the operator disengaged the ADS at `{python} IncidentRecord.t_takeover_math` [@ntsb2019uber].

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_tempe_suppression_strip.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A strip of five equal cells in time order, labeled in seconds before impact: detected at 5.6 seconds, emergency recognized at 1.2 seconds, a red cell for the one-second action suppression bracketed as 18.7 meters with the brake withheld, slowdown planned at 0.2 seconds, and operator takeover at 0.02 seconds. Cell widths are not to scale."}

*Detection, recognition, and braking were separate events; suppression spent `{python} IncidentRecord.d_suppress_str`.*
:::

The first term of the warehouse stopping budget applies directly. Averaging the two recorded speeds over the `{python} IncidentRecord.t_suppress_str` of suppression, the vehicle traveled about `{python} IncidentRecord.d_suppress_str` while emergency braking was withheld, distance that no later action could recover. The speed still fell during that second because a slowdown for the planned right turn at the next intersection was already under way; what the suppression withheld was the emergency response [@ntsb2019uber]. The emergency itself was defined by a chosen limit. The ADS treated a situation as an emergency when avoiding a collision required more than `{python} IncidentRecord.a_cap_str` (`{python} IncidentRecord.a_cap_g_str` g) of deceleration or a jerk[^fn-jerk-brake-ramp] beyond its limit, and it capped its own automated braking at that deceleration; police determined that the vehicle could decelerate at an average of `{python} IncidentRecord.g_capable_str` g, about `{python} IncidentRecord.a_capable_str`, on that road surface [@ntsb2019uber]. The difference between a chosen permission limit and a physical one is the distinction the book's numbers keep throughout. We do not extend the calculation to a counterfactual stop, because the report does not establish when a different design would have begun braking. Detection, correct path prediction, hazard recognition, and physical braking are distinct events; reporting the first detection time alone conceals the failures between them.

[^fn-jerk-brake-ramp]: **Jerk**: The rate of change of acceleration, in m/s³. A jerk limit makes a brake ramp its deceleration up instead of stepping it, which spares occupants, loads, and transmissions a shock but costs stopping distance, because full deceleration arrives later. The warehouse machine's card carries a jerk bound for the same reason, and the machine's finished stopping budget pays for the ramp. \index{Jerk!braking}

::: {#ws-boundary-missing-safety-referee .callout-war-story title="The disabled safety redundancy (2018)"}
**Context**: On March 18, 2018, a developmental ADS on a 2017 Volvo XC90 struck and killed a pedestrian crossing a road in Tempe, Arizona [@ntsb2019uber].

**Mechanism**: As traced above, classification changes discarded the object's tracking history, and the one-second suppression withheld braking until only a gradual slowdown was planned. The design did not use maximum braking solely to mitigate an unavoidable collision [@ntsb2019uber].

**Impact**: The vehicle struck and fatally injured the pedestrian. The late gradual-slowdown plan could not recover the lost stopping opportunity.

**Response**: The NTSB determined that the probable cause was the vehicle operator's failure to monitor the driving environment and the ADS because she was visually distracted throughout the trip by her personal cell phone. It found three contributing factors at Uber ATG, all a consequence of an inadequate safety culture: inadequate safety risk assessment procedures, ineffective oversight of vehicle operators, and a lack of adequate mechanisms for addressing operators' automation complacency. The impaired pedestrian's crossing outside a crosswalk and the Arizona Department of Transportation's insufficient oversight of automated vehicle testing also contributed. The NTSB further found that deactivating the Volvo collision warning and automatic emergency braking, which Uber ATG had done over possible radar interference, removed a layer of safety redundancy, and it recommended stronger safety risk management for testing automated vehicles [@ntsb2019uber].

**Systems lesson**: Classification uncertainty, a delayed response rule, and reliance on an inattentive operator can combine. The design made the operator the primary countermeasure in an emergency, yet no mechanism monitored her attention in real time: authority rested on evidence nobody collected. A design needs timely hazard assessment and a response that can mitigate impact when avoidance is no longer possible; the investigation does not prescribe a particular processor or mailbox architecture.
:::

The investigation supports a broader architectural requirement. A developmental ADS needs safety redundancy and a timely mitigation path even when perception or path prediction fails, and simulation tests by Volvo that the NTSB cites suggest that the factory emergency braking might have prevented or mitigated this collision. The report does not establish when a separate permission path would have triggered or where it would have stopped the vehicle.[^fn-std-safety-standards]

[^fn-std-safety-standards]: **Safety-Critical Standards**\index{Safety-Critical Standards!autonomous systems}: Three standards divide the ground. ISO 26262 addresses hazards caused by faults in a vehicle's electrical and electronic systems [@iso26262]; ISO 21448, safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF), addresses hazards that arise when a function works as designed but performs insufficiently, as perception can [@iso21448]; and UL 4600 sets out the safety case for autonomous products with no human driver to fall back on [@ul4600]. Tempe falls on the SOTIF side, since the recorded failures were in classification and path prediction rather than in a faulted component, and none of the three prescribes a processor architecture. The standards map maps the standards that govern the running machine.

Tempe illustrates failure *before* impact, where classification changes and a software suppression delay prevented timely braking. The 2023 Cruise robotaxi incident marks the opposite pole *after* impact. A hit-and-run driver's car threw a pedestrian into the path of the driverless vehicle, which braked hard but struck her and stopped. It then began a pullover toward a minimal-risk condition[^fn-mrc-fallback-motion] and, because its sensing did not detect a person beneath the vehicle, moved about `{python} IncidentRecord.d_drag_str` (`{python} IncidentRecord.d_drag_m_str`) at up to `{python} IncidentRecord.v_drag_str` while she was pinned beneath it. This account comes from a review commissioned by the company's boards, whose focus was the company's disclosures to regulators [@quinnemanuel2024cruise].

[^fn-mrc-fallback-motion]: **Minimal-Risk Condition**: In automated driving, the stable, usually stopped, state a system brings a vehicle to when a trip cannot or should not continue. Reaching it can itself require motion, as a pullover to the curb does, and in the Cruise case that motion was the harm. A fallback trajectory therefore needs the same permission check as any other proposal, judged against fresh evidence about the space it will move through. \index{Minimal-risk condition!fallback motion}

Neither failure reduces to an inaccurate model. The first spent stopping distance before braking began, and no later action could recover it. The second chose motion after the impact. Together they show what must hold before the machine acts and what a fallback may do once harm has begun. Both also had to be reconstructed afterward from records of what the machine perceived and when, so accountability, like safety, depends on the path that authorizes motion.

## Safety Convergence {#sec-boundary-safety-convergence}

In standard enterprise software and distributed systems, safety, security, and accountability are typically segregated into distinct operational tiers. Security defends network boundaries with cryptographic tokens; reliability frameworks mitigate component failures through retries and circuit breakers; accountability records remote procedure call (RPC) transactions to append-only databases. In physical AI, these three disciplines collapse directly onto the causal boundary—the interface where software commands meet physical actuators. Consider an autonomous mobile robot navigating a warehouse aisle at 3 m/s. The machine requires a valid stopping decision regardless of whether its forward cameras are obscured by dirt, an attacker has injected spoofed packets onto the internal Controller Area Network bus, or a vision-language-action policy has hallucinated an unobstructed path. In each case, the ultimate hazard is kinetic: an uncontrolled collision with infrastructure or human workers. Because physical momentum cannot be rolled back like a failed database transaction, admission control cannot simply confirm who dispatched a command. The system must determine whether executing that command right now violates physical safety invariants.

Consider how an ordinary environmental degradation challenges this boundary. If an autonomous forklift moves from dry concrete onto a patch of spilled hydraulic fluid, the friction coefficient between tire and floor can plunge from $0.8$ to $0.2$. Under maximum braking, the stopping distance quadruples. A clearance envelope and speed profile computed barely 100 ms earlier are immediately invalidated. The learned planner, processing visual camera streams that fail to reveal the transparent slick, may continue to output an aggressive velocity command with high nominal confidence. Safety verification cannot treat the model's internal confidence as proof of physical feasibility. Restricting machine operation demands independent, real-time evidence from the physical plant and its immediate environment—including wheel-slip telemetry, inertial measurement unit acceleration discrepancies, and motor current transients—to detect dynamic divergence and dynamically clamp actuator setpoints to a safe stopping profile.

Security threats target this same permission machinery by corrupting the evidence used to authorize motion. An adversary does not need to crack cryptographic keys or modify model weights to destabilize a physical agent; distorting the sensory inputs that inform admission decisions is sufficient. Projecting structured light patterns onto camera lenses, spoofing ultra-wideband localization beacons, or injecting rogue packets into sensor buses can deceive the controller into approving destructive commands, even while the neural network executes its inference pipeline without numerical fault. Isolating the proposer from the safety filter offers little defense if both subsystems ingest the same corrupted telemetry. Securing the causal boundary requires rigorous evidence validation: cross-verifying heterogeneous sensor streams (for example, corroborating camera-based visual odometry against wheel encoders and inertial sensors), enforcing cryptographic message authentication across bus transceivers, and maintaining fail-operational plausibility checks that reject sensor readings deviating from physical conservation laws.

In digital systems, a cryptographic capability token or access control list entry grants authority to modify a file regardless of processor load or ambient conditions. In physical AI, **physical authority is state-dependent.** Cryptographic credentials establish identity and organizational rights to request an action, but physical admissibility depends entirely on the instantaneous operational state of the machine and its workspace. A joint velocity command of 2 rad/s may represent a routine transit when an industrial manipulator operates in open free space, yet that identical command becomes unacceptable if the arm is within 2 mm of a mechanical hard stop or a human coworker. Evaluating physical authority requires testing the proposed action against instantaneous kinematics, payload inertia, motor thermal headroom, and state estimation uncertainty. Furthermore, admission control must remain coupled to an executable fallback. If the permission gate rejects a proposed command because the machine approaches an operational boundary, the controller must immediately dispatch a dynamically feasible contingency maneuver—such as controlled regenerative braking or compliant impedance control—that halts or redirects the plant without exceeding mechanical stress limits.

Accountability demands an audit trail that reconstructs the causal chain connecting sensory evidence to physical outcomes. When an embodied machine causes a collision or near-miss, post-incident analysis requires microsecond-level synchronization across multiple data streams: the raw observations ingested by the planner, the action proposed by the learned policy, the state estimates and dynamic constraints evaluated by the admission gate, the filtered command dispatched to the motor drives, and the measured response from joint encoders and force-torque sensors. Command logs record the intended trajectory, while sensor telemetry measures the plant's actual mechanical response. Recording dispatched setpoints alone does not confirm that an actuator executed them; an open-circuit fault, a tripped thermal breaker, or mechanical gearbox jamming will cause the physical plant to diverge immediately from commanded behavior. Both streams must be logged using synchronized hardware clocks (such as IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol) so that investigators can definitively distinguish between a planning failure, an admission gate error, and an electromechanical actuator breakdown.

Safety, security, and accountability ultimately converge on three unified demands at the permission path guarding the causal boundary:

1. Fresh, authenticated physical state: The permission gate must operate on telemetry fresh enough to bound physical uncertainty and robust enough against tampering or degradation to justify action admission.
2. Deterministic authority to intervene: The admission mechanism requires uncompromised physical authority to veto or clamp unfeasible proposals and inject safe contingency maneuvers, regardless of the learned model's internal confidence or identity.
3. Synchronous causal telemetry: The system must maintain an immutable record capturing what was proposed, what state was evaluated, what commands were dispatched, and how the physical machine responded.

The permission path is not merely a defensive software layer; it serves as the architectural foundation of embodied machine learning systems. By anchoring high-capacity, probabilistic neural policies to deterministic physical invariants, the permission path guarantees that physical AI delivers useful capabilities only under justified, provably safe operational bounds.

## The Four Bedrock Laws {#sec-boundary-bedrock-laws}

Manipulating an unfamiliar door latch or transporting an unmodeled payload requires far more than a sequence of statistically accurate model predictions. An embodied machine must respect the mechanical limits of its plant, adapt to dynamic environments altered by its own motion, and arbitrate between speculative model outputs and physically safe actuation. Four bedrock laws organize these engineering responsibilities, each anchoring a major part of this book:

**The first law: irreversibility.** Software cannot roll back physical consequences. In pure digital systems, an erroneous transaction can be aborted and state restored from a checkpoint. In physical space, however, work performed on a plant is thermodynamic and permanent. A motor command that collides with a fixture, tears a cable, or fractures a fragile payload cannot be retracted. Every admissibility check must therefore complete before the machine consumes its remaining clearance margin. As the stopping distance budget demonstrates, processing latency directly expends physical clearance, forcing the mechanical actuators to brake over an ever-shrinking distance. Reversing a drive voltage may eventually return an arm to its starting coordinates, but it cannot mend cracked structural material or recover energy lost to friction and heat. Part I translates this physical reality into kinetic budgets for the robot's body and deterministic timing constraints for its low-level controllers.

**The second law: endogenous data.** In classic offline machine learning, data samples are drawn independently from a stationary distribution. In embodied systems, data generation is strictly endogenous: every control action alters the physical state and determines what sensors will observe next. If an arm nudges an object during an approach, the object shifts; if a mobile base drifts off its nominal path, the subsequent visual frames deviate from the training demonstrations. Single-step prediction accuracy on an offline benchmark cannot guarantee closed-loop stability, because minor execution errors compound across the task horizon. Part II frames data collection, model training, and policy evaluation as a continuous improvement cycle: diagnose behavioral failures, curate targeted recovery demonstrations, retrain candidate policies, and systematically evaluate both performance gains and unintended regressions. Empirical evidence from past rollouts bounds what we can claim about present capability; only qualified new experience can expand that envelope.

**The third law: proposal is not permission.** A learned model operates strictly as a proposer, never as an unconstrained executor. An architecturally independent permission path—such as a runtime safety filter or an assurance monitor—must arbitrate every proposed control command before that command reaches hardware actuators. Granting permission requires three prerequisites: fresh state estimates from verified sensors, explicit mathematical guarantees that the command respects all physical safety envelopes, and an immediately executable fallback maneuver if the proposal is delayed, missing, or unsafe. This separation of authority must remain robust against system faults: a runaway or stalled model thread must never be allowed to delay, starve, or corrupt the deterministic safety logic guarding the plant. Part III constructs the real-time execution runtime around this strict division between speculative proposal and certified permission.

**The fourth law: evidence bounds authority.** An embodied machine's legitimate operational authority extends only as far as the empirical evidence supporting its performance under stated conditions. Flawless execution across a handful of laboratory trials does not justify autonomy across diverse surface friction, variable payloads, degraded lighting, or sensor degradation. Every deployment safety case must explicitly demarcate the system's operational design domain (ODD),[^fn-odd-evidence-scope] articulate the environmental assumptions underlying those boundaries, and specify fail-safe degradation policies whenever runtime conditions drift beyond verified bounds. The 2018 Uber ATG collision in Tempe, Arizona, tragically demonstrated the cost of ignoring this boundary: the system architecture relied on an in-vehicle safety operator as the primary emergency countermeasure, yet lacked any mechanism to monitor whether the operator was actually attending to the roadway [@ntsb2019uber]. Part IV formalizes command authority, fault injection testing, and release criteria so that epistemic and physical uncertainty strictly circumscribe what the machine is permitted to do.

[^fn-odd-evidence-scope]: **Operational Design Domain (ODD)**: The automated-driving name for the stated environmental and operational conditions—such as roadway types, speed ranges, weather, and lighting—under which a system is designed to operate, and the foundational scope of a UL 4600 safety case [@ul4600]. This book applies the concept to the payloads, surface friction, operating velocities, and dynamic disturbances covered by the machine's empirical validation. Operating outside that verified domain rests on no evidentiary basis whatever, which is why later chapters structures the operating domain as an explicit scenario ledger against which collected training data are audited. \index{Operational design domain!evidence}

Among these four mandates, only the first is an immutable physical law. Irreversibility arises directly from Newtonian mechanics and thermodynamics: work performed on a plant transfers energy and alters physical entropy, and no software architecture can undo that state transition. The remaining three are engineering design principles. They embody hard-won lessons forged through decades of systems engineering, industrial robotics, and aerospace failures. An engineering team could theoretically build an architecture that violates them—for example, by piping unvalidated neural network outputs straight to motor amplifiers—but doing so incurs severe, predictable risks. We elevate all four to the status of bedrock laws because this book treats them as mandatory constraints for any production embodied system.

None of these three architectural principles is entirely novel. Each has a rich foundation in computer systems, control theory, and safety-critical engineering. @Tbl-01-law-lineage maps this book's terminology to the established literature, alongside the canonical sources and documented real-world failures each principle distills—including the Tempe and Cruise incidents. Where our terms introduce tighter operational precision, as when tying state freshness directly to the dynamic stopping budget, we retain specialized systems phrasing; when searching broader engineering literature, the classical terms serve as the standard index.

| Book's law or term                                                         | Kind             | Established name in the field                                             | Canonical source                                               | Documented failure it distills                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| First law: irreversibility (the causal boundary)                           | Physical         | Irreversible work on the plant; the reaction-plus-braking stopping budget | Mechanics; later chapters                          | Tempe (2018): the one-second action suppression let the vehicle travel about `{python} IncidentRecord.d_suppress_str` with emergency braking withheld [@ntsb2019uber]                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Second law: endogenous data                                                | Design principle | Covariate shift; compounding error in imitation learning                  | Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell [@ross2011reduction]                 | A learning result rather than an accident: a cloned policy's errors can compound with the task horizon (later chapters)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Third law: proposal is not permission (proposal boundary, permission path) | Design principle | Runtime assurance and its Simplex architecture; safety filter             | Sha [@sha2001using]; Hsu, Hu, and Fisac [@hsu2024safetyfilter] | Therac-25: software took over protection that hardware interlocks had provided [@leveson1993investigating]; Mars Pathfinder (1997): through priority inversion, lower-priority work delayed a deadline-critical bus task until the scheduler's completion check reset the computer [@reeves1997pathfinder]                                                             |
| Fresh evidence (an input to every permission check)                        | Design principle | Age of information                                                        | Kaul, Yates, and Gruteser [@kaul2012realtime]                  | While not a pure staleness failure, Tempe (2018) shows the neighboring hazard of discarded evidence: each object reclassification dropped historical tracks, forcing path prediction to compute trajectories on truncated sensor history [@ntsb2019uber]                                                                                                               |

: **Lineage of the four laws**: Each law and key term of this book against the field's established name, its canonical source, and a documented failure it distills. Only the first law is physical; the other three are design principles, which is why each has an independent literature. Runtime assurance enters with the proposal boundary, and @sec-boundary-history traces its lineage together with the safety filter and the assurance case. {#tbl-01-law-lineage tbl-colwidths="[20,10,20,16,34]"}

The proposal boundary unifies these four laws into an integrated systems architecture. Irreversibility dictates that safety checks execute before any physical command alters plant state. Endogenous data explains why offline training metrics alone cannot guarantee closed-loop stability. Evidence boundaries establish the verified operational limits within which autonomous proposals remain justified.

Scaling up model capacity does not relax these constraints; on the contrary, it intensifies physical pressure on the system. Although general machine learning methods deliver superior performance as compute expands [@sutton2019bitter], an embodied agent must carry its compute infrastructure onboard. Every additional neural layer, attention head, or diffusion step draws against fixed physical allocations of memory bandwidth, electrical power, and thermal dissipation. Crucially, inference latency translates directly into unrecoverable braking distance: every millisecond spent waiting for a deep network to evaluate a forward pass burns clearance that the mechanical brakes can never reclaim. This compute, thermal, and temporal ceiling forms the physical wall confronting every learned proposer.

Finally, rejecting an inadmissible command must have an explicit physical realization. In traditional software, an unhandled exception or failed assertion can simply terminate a thread. On a moving robot, halting a software process leaves physical momentum untouched. A refusal is meaningful only if the execution runtime immediately dispatches an admissible fallback—whether a dynamic braking maneuver, an impedance-controlled hold, or a controlled stop—that the physical body can safely execute within its remaining stopping clearance. Translating these four laws and their runtime mechanisms into an engineered system requires a disciplined progression across the four parts of this book.

## The Architecture of This Book {#sec-boundary-book-architecture}

Moving a learned proposal—such as a mobile manipulator's trajectory to open a warehouse cage door—from an abstract task requirement to safe, justified physical operation requires a disciplined four-stage progression. The engineer must first bound what the hardware plant can physically achieve, characterize what the learned proposer has demonstrated under rigorous testing, build an isolated runtime monitor to intercept live proposals, and establish the operational conditions under which continued execution remains justified. Each stage corresponds to one of the book's four governing laws. The system of records illustrated in @fig-01-spine formalizes this progression, capturing operating assumptions and empirical evidence so that downstream runtime decisions can inspect and rely on them. Conceptually, these records trace two converging pipelines. One strand establishes offline physical limits and verified competence; the second processes online sensor observations and real-time candidate actions. Both pipelines converge at the permission decision, where the system admits or rejects a proposed trajectory. Ultimately, this architecture synthesizes both strands to resolve the book's central challenge: engineering dependable, high-performance physical systems out of unverified learned models and unforgiving mechanical hardware.

A record is a machine-checkable artifact that downstream safety and runtime decisions can verify and trust. The initial stopping calculation (notebook \ref{nbk-boundary-stopping-budget}) already sketches the outline of our first milestone: a limit record containing the six core elements introduced in the reader guide. Its nominal value is the derived stopping distance. Its operational conditions specify the payload mass, dry concrete, a stationary obstacle, and a constant approach speed. At this stage, however, its uncertainty remains unquantified because the inputs are illustrative scalars rather than calibrated empirical distributions. Consequently, the apparent buffer between the obstacle and the machine is simply an arithmetic difference between provisional figures rather than a verified safety margin. The system also lacks a runtime detector; no sensor on the machine currently monitors whether floor traction drops or cargo shifts outside the assumed envelope. The schema for the limit record specifies the runtime detector a limit record requires. Finally, its provenance consists solely of baseline assumptions rather than calibrated hardware logs. These omissions highlight an essential systems principle: an ungrounded calculation becomes operational engineering evidence only when all six fields are populated and backed by empirical data. Every numbered box across the four part bands in @fig-01-spine establishes a machine-checkable record of this rigor for a distinct architectural decision.

::: {#fig-01-spine fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The spine of the book**: Each part is led by one law, and each chapter of Parts I to IV except the chapter on the brain produces a record that a later one consumes. What the plant can do and what the proposer has shown it can do run as one strand, what the proposer proposes now as another, and the two meet at the permission decision." fig-alt="Flow diagram of fifteen record boxes, each labeled with its chapter number, on shaded bands for the four parts. A label at top left reads Chapter 1, What must be guaranteed. In the Part I band, labeled Irreversibility, the limit record of Chapter 2 feeds the handoff record of Chapter 4, and a dashed arrow labeled Chapter 3, proposer limits, also enters the handoff record. The handoff record forks into two rows. The upper row, in the Part II band labeled Endogenous data, runs provenance record 5, policy manifest 6, and evaluation record 7. The lower row, in the Part III band labeled Proposal is not permission, runs observation contract 8, belief record 9, intent lease 10, and trajectory record 11. Both rows converge on the enforcement record of Chapter 12, which feeds the placement record of Chapter 13. An arrow then runs down to a lower row in the Part IV band, labeled Evidence bounds authority: authority record 14, fault record 15, and release manifest 16, which feeds the residual-claims register of Chapter 17, labeled Conclusion and What the evidence supports. A separate arrow runs from the evaluation record around the top and right edges to the release manifest."}
